studyData.intro: This English-language Tokyo edition places a small framed cat between a large red title and two translation credits. Read its face and whiskers closely, then distinguish this object from the better-known Japanese covers of other volumes.

regions.label: Red English title
regions.summary: A first-person statement opens the cover.

sections.heading: The animal says I
sections.body: The visible title is I AM A CAT. The first-person wording invites the pictured animal to be read as a speaking presence, but the cover does not need a human narrator’s portrait to establish that grammatical voice.

sections.heading: A particular translated edition
sections.body: Yale dates this English Hattori Shoten volume to 1906–1909 and locates publication in Tokyo. It is not the Japanese 1905 first volume, so a designer credit associated with that different object is not assumed here.

regions.question: How does the title change your encounter with the cat’s direct gaze?

regions.label: Frontal cat face
regions.kicker: A FACE HELD NEAR THE CENTRE
regions.summary: Dark and light marks create a direct encounter.

sections.heading: A face held near the centre
sections.body: The cat faces forward inside a small rectangular picture. Dark patches around the eyes and nose contrast with pale fur shapes, while the close spacing of the features gives the head a concentrated, attentive appearance.

sections.heading: Small image, strong presence
sections.body: Although the illustration occupies only a fraction of the cover, the frontal face can hold attention against the much larger paper field. Its visual force comes from contrast and orientation rather than from sheer size.

regions.question: Would a profile cat have the same relationship with the first-person title?

regions.label: Pointed ears
regions.summary: Two angled tips widen the face.

sections.heading: An outward pair
sections.body: The ears rise to either side of the head and lean outward. Their pointed silhouettes contrast with the rounder cheek and eye shapes, making the upper part of the cat easy to recognise inside the tight frame.

sections.heading: A rhythm above the eyes
sections.body: The ear tips form a wide pair above the narrower facial features. This nesting of wide and narrow shapes gives the little portrait internal structure, even before individual fur marks are examined.

regions.question: Which pair spreads farther across the picture: the ears, the eyes or the whiskers?

regions.label: Whiskers reaching the frame
regions.summary: Fine lines extend beyond the central face.

sections.heading: Thin strokes in pale space
sections.body: Long whisker lines run from the muzzle toward the picture boundary. They are finer than the dark body patches, so the pale intervals around them are essential to their legibility. Several reach close to the actual frame.

sections.heading: A scale change within one image
sections.body: The whiskers make the viewer move from a broad animal silhouette to very small marks. Their delicacy contrasts with the blunt red title above, giving the cover more than one level of visual attention.

regions.question: What is lost if the whiskers are reduced to the same thickness as the body patches?

regions.label: Ink body patches
regions.summary: Irregular shapes keep the cat from becoming a flat icon.

sections.heading: Dark islands and pale channels
sections.body: Below the face, broken dark patches suggest the chest and forelegs. Pale channels divide these areas, so the animal is built from alternating light and dark shapes rather than a single filled silhouette.

sections.heading: Texture inside a compact frame
sections.body: The irregular patches introduce variety within the orderly rectangular boundary. They can suggest fur and volume while still reading as printed marks, preserving a difference between the cat and its surrounding frame.

regions.question: Do the pale channels look like empty paper, light fur, or both?

regions.label: Printed picture frame
regions.summary: A small boundary organises a large cover.

sections.heading: An uneven rectangle
sections.body: The dark border encloses the cat with rounded and slightly irregular corners. It is visibly printed rather than mechanically perfect, and it stays distinct from the much larger worn outer edge of the book.

sections.heading: A portrait within an object
sections.body: The frame turns the cat into a compact central picture, leaving generous paper above and below for words. That separation lets the cover alternate between reading language and looking at an image.

regions.question: Would the cat feel larger if its frame disappeared while the drawing stayed the same size?

regions.label: Small adjacent mark
regions.summary: A tiny mark asks for restraint.

sections.heading: A compact dark detail
sections.body: A small dark mark sits near the lower-right side of the cat image. It is much smaller than the main printed words and belongs visually with the framed picture rather than the red credit lines below.

sections.heading: What the source does not establish
sections.body: The consulted Yale catalogue does not identify this particular cover artist. The tiny mark is therefore not expanded into a guessed signature or used to transfer an attribution from another edition of the novel.

regions.question: What evidence would you want before reading a tiny mark as an artist’s signature?

regions.label: Translator credit
regions.summary: Translation is given its own visible line.

sections.heading: A named act of translation
sections.body: The lower red line reads TRANSLATED BY K. ANDO. Its smaller capitals distinguish this role from the large title, while the repeated red colour keeps the two verbal areas connected across the intervening portrait.

sections.heading: An English edition published in Tokyo
sections.body: Yale records English as the language, Hattori Shoten as publisher and Tokyo as publication place. The visible translation credit is therefore useful edition information; English wording alone would not establish a British or American publishing context.

regions.question: How does this credit help distinguish the work’s language of origin from the language of this object?

regions.label: Separate revision credit
regions.kicker: REVISION IS NOT THE SAME LINE
regions.summary: A second role follows the translator.

sections.heading: Revision is not the same line
sections.body: REVISED BY K. NATSUME appears beneath the translation line. Keeping the two statements separate makes two forms of textual work visible, even though the cover uses the same red colour and similar-sized lettering for both.

sections.heading: A two-step ending
sections.body: The lower lines form a small stack with a narrow interval between them. They finish the cover more quietly than the title, but their alignment creates a strong base beneath the central picture.

regions.question: Would combining both names in one line obscure the difference between their stated roles?

regions.label: Worn paper field
regions.summary: A broad tan surface surrounds the picture.

sections.heading: The surface is not uniform
sections.body: Stains, rubbed areas and folds vary across the tan paper. Much of this surface remains unprinted, especially beside the portrait, allowing the small black image and red words to remain clearly separated.

sections.heading: A surviving object, not a cleaned design
sections.body: The Yale reproduction preserves the condition of a specific volume dated 1906–1909. Wear is retained here as part of that record; it is not interpreted as a deliberate colour pattern or removed to simulate an imagined new copy.

regions.question: Which features describe the original arrangement, and which describe this copy’s survival?
